# OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

## BOOK THREE.

<image-desc>A horizontal divider made of repeating decorative circular floral patterns.</image-desc>

### CHAPTER ONE.

->*On the necessity, power, and utility of Religion.*<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter "I" decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

It is now time for us to occupy ourselves with more elevated subjects, and to attach our spirit to that part of <term>Magic</term> <note>Here referring to "Ceremonial Magic," the highest branch of the occult sciences dealing with the divine</note> which teaches us to seek out and know the laws and ceremonies of religions. We must learn how we ought to grasp the truth through divine religion, and how—following religious ceremonies—we may form and exercise our spirit and our reason. It is by these alone that we are able to comprehend the truth; for it is the consensus of all the <term>Mages</term> <note>The "Magi" or wise men of antiquity who studied the hidden laws of the universe</note> that if the spirit and the reason are not

<summary>This introductory page marks the beginning of the third book, shifting the focus from natural and celestial magic to the spiritual necessity of religion and divine ceremony. The author argues that human reason can only attain ultimate truth through the structured practice of religious laws.</summary>
<keywords>Occult Philosophy, Ceremonial Magic, Divine Truth, Religious Rites, Reason and Spirit, Mages</keywords>

# PHILOSOPHY

are in good condition, the body cannot be; that man is truly healthy when the soul and the body are so well united, and so well in accord, that the forces of the spirit and of reason are not inferior to those of the body. Now, we cannot, according to the opinion of Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note>, have this firmness and vigor of spirit from anywhere else but from the purity of life, from piety, and from divine or religious service; for the holiness of religion purifies the spirit and fills it with God. Religion also comes to the aid of nature; it strengthens its forces just as the physician strengthens the health of the body, and as the farmer increases the fertility of the earth.

Evil spirits very often deceive those who neglect religion and attach themselves only to nature; one finds in the knowledge of religion the contempt for and the remedy against vices, and protection against evil spirits. Finally, nothing is more agreeable nor better received before God than the man who is perfectly pious and truly religious; he is as much above all other men as the immortal Gods are above him. We must therefore, after having well prepared ourselves by a good life, present ourselves and give ourselves over to the love of God and to religion; and in this state, in a slumber of all the senses <note>A reference to a meditative or ecstatic state where physical senses are quieted to allow spiritual perception.</note> and a tranquility of spirit, await that divine ambrosia, that divine nectar; nectar, I say, which the Prophet Zechariah calls a wine that makes the virgins bear fruit <note>original: "vin qui fait porter fruit aux vierges" — a reference to Zechariah 9:17.</note>, praising and adoring the Bacchus <note>The author here syncretizes the Greek god Bacchus/Dionysus with a higher celestial principle or perhaps a Christ-figure, common in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> raised above the heavens, the Sovereign of the Gods, the King of the Priesthood, the author of regeneration celebrated by the ancient Prophets under the title of "twice-born" <note>original: "deux fois né" — translating the Greek 'Dionysus' or 'dimetor', referring to his mythological rebirth, here used as a metaphor for spiritual rebirth.</note>, from whom we receive divine gifts.

# OCCULT, Book III.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning silence, and the concealment of those things which constitute mysteries and secrets in Religion.

WHOSOEVER you may be who wish to devote yourself to this science, keep under a religious silence in the depths of your heart, like a secret of religion, a doctrine so sacred, and conceal it with an unshakable constancy, which never permits you to speak of it; for, as Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism</note> says, it is an offense against religion to confide to many a discourse so filled with the majesty of God; and the divine Plato forbade publishing among the common people the sacrament <note>original: "sacrement," here meaning a holy rite or mystery</note> and the secrets contained within the mysteries. Pythagoras likewise and Porphyry obliged their disciples to a religious secrecy; in the same way, Orpheus required from those he received into the ceremonies of sacred things an oath of silence, through a kind of trembling reverence to prevent the mysteries of religion from reaching the ears of the unworthy and profane populace: This is why, in his hymn of the sacred word <note>original: "verbe sacré," likely referring to the Orphic 'Hieros Logos'</note> to the partisans of virtue, he speaks in these terms: *You friends of virtue, it is you whom I exhort to listen only to my words, and to strain your minds; on the contrary, you who despise sacred things, the laws, and ceremonies of religion, withdraw from here promptly; withdraw far from here, you wretches; go far away from our places.*

# O C C U L T, Book III.

By keeping silence, then, and hiding those things which are secrets in religion, we shall thus make disciples worthy of this science: For as **Tertullian** <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), an early Christian author from Carthage.</note> says, one is obliged to keep the faith of silence in religions; those who do otherwise are on the edge of a precipice. From this comes the precaution of **Apuleius** <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124 – c. 170 AD), a Roman philosopher and author known for "The Golden Ass," which deals with the mysteries of Isis.</note> regarding the mysteries of sacred things: *I would reveal the mysteries to you if it were permitted for me to tell them, and I would give you the knowledge of them if it were permitted for you to listen; but both I who spoke, and you who listened, would be equally punished for our rash curiosity.* For a similar fault, we find in history that **Theodorus**, a tragic poet, was struck with blindness for wanting to apply certain things from the mysteries of the Jewish scriptures to some fable. Likewise, **Theopompus**, who had begun to translate some verses of the Divine Law into Greek, was confounded and lost his mind in a moment; it was for this reason that, following his misfortune, addressing God with great prayers to know the cause of this accident, he was answered in a dream that it was because he was making a criminal trade of divine things by exposing them to public profanation. Similarly, a certain **Numenius**, curious about secrets, became a criminal before the Gods for having communicated the sacred mysteries of the goddess of **Eleusis** <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious rites of ancient Greece centered on Demeter and Persephone.</note> to the public through the interpretation he had made of them; for he saw in a dream the Eleusinian goddesses exposed at the open door of a brothel in the clothes of harlots, and as he looked on in wonder at this state, they replied to him in anger that he had dragged them

# OCCULT PHILOSOPHY, Book III;

...several great mysteries, and the most significant sacraments of <term>ceremonial magic</term> <note>Magic involving complex rituals, invocations, and religious observances to contact spiritual beings.</note>. I believe that I will have done enough by having reported to you the things necessary to know, and that you might draw from the reading of these books some knowledge of these mysteries; but remember that they are communicated to you only under the condition to which **Dionysius** <note>original: "Denis"; likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings on celestial hierarchies were foundational to Renaissance occultism.</note> bound **Timothy** <note>original: "Thimotée"; Saint Timothy, the companion of Paul, to whom Dionysius addressed his work "The Divine Names."</note>: which is that those who understand these mysteries do not make them known to the unworthy, but that these sacred secrets, retained among a small number of the wise, be kept with the reverence due to them. Furthermore, at the beginning of this book, I wish to warn you of this point of importance: that just as the divinities detest things exposed to the public and profaned, and as they love, on the contrary, things that are distinguished and singular; so every experience of magic abhors the public, seeks to be hidden, is strengthened by silence, and is destroyed by declaration; the complete effect does not follow [exposure]; for one loses all these advantages by exposing them to chatterers and the incredulous. It is necessary, therefore, that an operator in the matter of Magic, if he wishes to profit from it, be secret, and that he tell no one of his work, nor the place, nor the time, nor what he desires, nor his will—except to his master, or to his coadjutor or associate, who must also be faithful, believing, and taciturn, and worthy of this science, either by nature or by instruction; because the excessive talking even of a partner, his incredulity, and his unworthiness hinders every operation and causes the effect to miscarry.

# CHAPTER III.

## *What dignity is necessary to become a true Magician and a worker of wonders.*

At the beginning of the first book of this work, we spoke of the qualities a Magician must possess, but now we shall speak of the <term>arcane</term> <note>From the Latin *arcanum*, meaning a profound secret or a mystery known only to initiates.</note> matter, necessary and secret to anyone who wishes to operate in this art. This arcane matter is the hope for fulfillment and the key to all magical operations: it is the very <term>dignification</term> <note>In Renaissance magic, this refers to the spiritual purification and exaltation of the soul, making the practitioner "worthy" to command spiritual forces.</note> of man through such high virtue and power. This faculty requires an admirable dignity in man; for it is only the <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "entendement"; in this context, it refers to the *Intellectus*, the highest faculty of the human soul which is capable of direct spiritual perception beyond mere logic.</note> itself—which is within us the most sovereign intelligence of the soul—that can alone perform miraculous works, provided it is not too entangled in the commerce of the flesh, but rather occupied with divine things.

This is the reason why many people seek this sort of Magic without finding it. It is therefore necessary that we, who aspire to such a high dignity, think of two things: first, by what means we shall detach ourselves from the affections of the flesh, from the mortal senses, and from the passions of matter and the body; the other, by what path and how we shall elevate ourselves to this pure understanding, which is attached to the virtues of the Gods. Without this, we can never happily arrive at the knowledge of secret things, or at the virtue of—

<summary>This chapter introduces the concept of spiritual "dignification," arguing that a magician's power comes from an intellect purified of physical passions and elevated to a divine level. It sets the stage for practical instructions on how to detach from the material world to achieve miraculous results.</summary>

Natural dignity is an excellent disposition of the body and of all its parts, which does not obscure the lights of the soul by any blemish, and which causes it no tumult nor movement of the <term>humors</term> <note>original: "humeurs"; according to ancient medicine, these were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—that governed health and temperament.</note>; and this excellent disposition of the body and its organs comes from the situation, the movement, the light, and the influence of the celestial bodies and souls that preside over the birth of each person. Such are those whose <term>ninth house</term> <note>In astrology, the ninth house of a birth chart traditionally governs religion, philosophy, and higher wisdom.</note> is fortunate by Saturn, the Sun, and Mercury; likewise, Mars in the ninth house presides over spirits. These things are treated at sufficient length in the books of Astrology. 

He who is not of such a happy constitution needs to supply the defect of nature through education, a very regulated life, and a good use of the things that succeed for him, until he is perfected in both the interior and the exterior. From this comes the reason why so much precaution was taken in the choice of a Priest in the <term>Mosaic law</term> <note>The religious laws of the ancient Israelites found in the Torah.</note>: it was necessary that he had not approached a dead body, a widow, or a woman during her period; that he was not a leper, nor subject to a flux of blood, nor to <term>ruptures</term> <note>original: "deſcentes"; likely referring to hernias or similar physical ailments.</note>; that he be healthy and whole in all his members—not blind, nor lame, nor hunchbacked, nor with a deformed nose. 

And <term>Apuleius</term> <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author, best known for his work *The Golden Ass* and his legal defense, the *Apology*, against charges of practicing magic.</note> in his *Apology* says that the child one wishes to make a diviner by enchantment must be chosen healthy, without defect, ingenious, well-made, whole, industrious, and eloquent, so that the divine power may be lodged in his person as in a good dwelling, and so that the spirit of this child, having become an expert in a short time, may be restored to divinity. It is therefore necessary, as was said at the beginning of the first book, to be learned and expert in those three faculties of which we have spoken <note>Agrippa refers to the three divisions of occult philosophy: Natural, Mathematical (Celestial), and Religious.</note>; then, once the obstacles are removed, one must give their soul entirely to contemplation, and enclose it within itself, because we naturally have within ourselves the power to understand and dispose of things, but we are troubled in the enjoyment of these things by the passions which present an obstacle to us from the side of <term>generation</term> <note>original: "generation"; referring here to the physical nature and bodily inclinations inherited through birth.</note>, and of birth by false imaginings and unruly appetites; divine knowledge and power present themselves as soon as these obstacles cease. I mean primarily that kind of superstition which has a certain resemblance to religion, which, insofar as it imitates everything within religion regarding miracles, sacraments, ceremonies, observances, and all other solemnities, gains no little authority from all this, and draws no less strength from the <term>credulity</term> <note>In this context, "credulity" is a technical term for a powerful, unshakeable psychological belief that Agrippa identifies as the "engine" of magical effects.</note> of the officiant. Superstition therefore demands credulity, just as religion requires faith, since constant credulity has so much power that it operates, and even works miracles in false opinions and operations; for every person in their religion, however false, provided they believe it to be true, raises their spirit according to the strength [of their belief...]

WE have three guides in matters of religion, who lead us even to the path of truth, who regulate all religion, and who form its entire foundation; and these three guides are love, hope, and faith; for love is the <term>vehicle of the soul</term> <note>Likely referring to the Neoplatonic *okhema*, a subtle body or "chariot" that allows the soul to interact with the material and spiritual realms.</note>; it is the pearl above all other virtues; coming forth from the high places, it descends from the <term>intelligences</term> <note>In the hierarchy of the universe, "Intelligences" refer to the celestial spirits or angels that govern the planetary spheres.</note> down to those most lowly, spreading its benefits everywhere. It adorns our spirit with so many ornaments that it makes it equal to the beauty of God, and deifies it; it preserves us in every operation, and causes the effects to succeed according to our wishes, giving strength and virtue to our prayers; as we read in Homer, that Apollo heard the prayer of his priest <note>original: "Chrises"</note> Chryses, because he loved him much; and we read again in the Gospels, concerning the Magdalene, that a great number of sins were forgiven her because she loved much. <note>This refers to the biblical passage in Luke 7:47: "Her many sins have been forgiven, for she loved much."</note>

As for the hope that is fixed firmly upon what it seeks, so long as it does not doubt and remains unshakable, it will nourish the spirit and perfect it, enfolding all things particularly within the <term>Good</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, "The Good" refers to the ultimate source of all reality and value.</note>.

Faith is indeed the source of all miracles; it is this alone, according to the opinion of the Platonicians, which allows us to approach God and obtain His protection and His blessing for virtue. It is by faith that we read in the Scripture that Daniel was saved from the mouth of the lions because he had firm confidence in his God. # CHAPTER VI.

## **How the soul, assisted by these guides, rises to the divine nature and becomes a worker of miracles.**

OUR soul having thus rendered itself pure and divinized; warmed by the love of God, adorned with hope, and led by faith, positioned upon the height and the summit of the human spirit, attracts truth to itself. In divine truth itself—as if in the mirror of eternity—it sees the state of both natural and supernatural and divine things, their essences, their causes, and the fullness of knowledge <note>original: "sciences"; in this context, it refers to the complete systems of wisdom and understanding rather than modern empirical science.</note>, comprehending everything in an instant. From this it follows that, when we are in this state of purity and elevation, we know things that are above nature, and we understand everything that is in this lower world; and we know not only present things and those that are past, but we also incessantly receive the oracles of what must soon happen, and of what will only happen a long time hereafter. Furthermore, an spirit of this quality acquires a divine virtue not only in the sciences, arts, and oracles, but it also receives a miraculous power in all things transmutable by command. From this it follows that, being established in nature, we sometimes dominate nature, and perform such miracu-

# CHAPTER VII.

### *On the necessity of the Magician’s knowledge of the true God, and of the sentiment that ancient Magicians and Philosophers held regarding divinity.*

SINCE all creatures can neither exist nor act without the cooperation of God, their sovereign Creator, and—after God—they also depend upon other deities who have received from God the power to fabricate and create, not as the primary cause, but as the final and instrumental cause through the virtue of the Creator; for He is the principle and the first cause of all things. However, that which is produced by secondary causes <note>In the philosophy of the time, "secondary causes" refers to intermediate forces—like angels, planets, or laws of nature—that carry out God's will.</note> is more effectively produced by the first cause, which also produced the secondary causes that we call the Gods of the second order <note>This term refers to celestial beings or "intelligences" that govern the heavens under the authority of the supreme Creator.</note>. It is therefore necessary that every Magician know the true God, who drew all things from nothingness and produced them as the first cause, and that he also know the other gods, deities, or superior powers that we call secondary causes. One must also know with what worship, what veneration, and what sacrifices—conforming to the condition, etc., of each—they must be recognized and honored, every one in particular: For whoever invokes the gods and does not render them the honor that has [appertained]—

## CHAPTER IX.

### *Concerning the true orthodox faith that we must hold toward God, and the most holy Trinity.*

THE Catholic Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to the "Doctors of the Church," eminent theologians whose teachings are considered authoritative.</note> and the faithful people have ordained that it is necessary to believe and confess that there is only one single and true God, uncreated <note>original: *incrée*; existing without having been created, a fundamental attribute of the Divine in theology.</note>, infinite, almighty, and eternal: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; three persons, in truth all three eternal and equal among themselves, who nonetheless constitute but a single essence and substance, and an absolutely simple nature. This is the Catholic faith, this is the orthodox religion, and this is the truth of Christianity: that we worship one God in the Trinity, and the Trinity in the unity of a God, without confounding the persons nor dividing the substance. 

The Father from all eternity has begotten his Son and given him His substance, and nevertheless He has retained it; the Son likewise, in being born, has received the substance of the Father. He has not, however, taken the Father’s own substance, nor has the Father transferred it into the Son; for they are both of one and the same substance, but they are distinct persons. The Son likewise, although eternal like the Father and begotten of the substance of the Father before all ages, was nonetheless born of the substance of the Virgin in time, and He was named Jesus,

It is therefore necessary that we believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, is God and man all at once: one person in him, and two natures. He is a God begotten before all ages <note>original: *devant tous les siècles*; refers to the eternal existence of Christ before the creation of time.</note>, without a mother; and in time he was made man without a father, born of a pure virgin both before and after the childbearing. Having suffered on the cross, he died, but he restored life upon the cross and delivered us from death through death. He was buried and descended into hell <note>In this context, "hell" (enfers) refers to the "Harrowing of Hell" or Limbo, where the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection were said to wait.</note>, but from there he delivered the souls of the ancient Patriarchs; he rose again on the third day by his own power. He ascended into the heavens and sent his Holy Spirit the Comforter; he will come to judge the living and the dead, and at his coming all men shall rise again in their flesh and render an account of their own deeds. This is the true faith; if anyone does not believe it, or if anyone doubts it, he is outside the paths of life and eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER X.

### *Of the divine emanations that the Hebrews call numerations, others call attributes, the gentiles call gods and deities; together with the ten Sephiroth, and the ten most sacred names of God, which preside over them, and their interpretation.*

ALTHOUGH God himself exists in three persons of a most unified essence, we nevertheless do not doubt that there are within Him certain deities in great number, which the Philosophers have called the gods of the gentiles <note>The "gentiles" here refers to the ancient Pagans (Greeks, Romans, etc.) who worshipped a pantheon of gods.</note>, the Doctors of the Hebrews call <term>numerations</term> <note>original: *numerations*; this is a literal translation of the Hebrew word *Sephiroth*, which refers to the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself.</note>, and we call attributes. These include wisdom, which Orpheus calls Pallas; understanding, which he calls Mercury; the production of form, which he calls Saturn; His procreative power, which he calls Neptune; the secret nature of things, which he calls Juno; love, which he calls Venus; the lucid life, which he calls the Sun or Apollo; and the reason of the universal world, which he calls Pan. As for the soul, he proclaims it through his song under these three names: Mars, Neptune, and Ocean—explaining how it produces the creatures of this lower world, how it also contemplates the higher realms, how it returns into itself, and several other things that he says elsewhere.

It is thus that these theologians of the <term>gentiles</term> <note>In this context, "gentiles" refers to the ancient Greeks and Romans who practiced polytheistic religions.</note> who conducted themselves with great prudence, honored God under different names, and also under both sexes. Mortal men, says Pliny, overburdened with pains and labors, have made several gods out of one in remembrance of their weakness, so that there being several gods to share and choose from, as if by way of portions, each might seek the favor of the one he needed most. Thus, those who needed faith invoked Jupiter; those who needed foresight invoked Apollo; those who needed wisdom called upon Minerva, and those who needed other things asked for them from their gods under other names. This diversity of so many kinds of divinities came from the weakness and the embarrassment of men, who needed to receive graces in quantity and of several kinds according to their needs; but there is only one sovereign God, the dispenser of all graces and of all things. ## CHAPTER XI.

### *On the names of God, and of their power and virtue.*

ALTHOUGH God is infinitely one, and one in his being; he nevertheless bears several names, which do not represent several different essences, or divinities, but through these sacred names, as if through channels, he causes a quantity of benefits, gifts, and graces to flow upon us. We have just given the description of ten of these names in the previous chapter, of which Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> likewise gave an account to Marcella; Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work *On the Divine Names*.</note> collected forty-five of them, pertaining as much to God the Father as to Jesus Christ. The *Mecubales* <note>A term for Kabbalists, derived from the Hebrew *Mequbalim*, meaning "those who have received" the tradition.</note>, or Doctors of the Hebrews, derive from a certain text in Exodus <note>Specifically Exodus 14:19–21, where each verse contains 72 letters, used to derive the 72 names.</note> seventy-two names of both God and the angels, which they call the "name of seventy-two letters," and *Shem HaMephorash* <note>original: *schemchamphoras*</note>, that is to say, explanatory or interpretative. Others, pushing further, report so many divine names from every passage of Scripture that we are entirely ignorant of their number and meaning. Among these names, besides those we have reported, is the name of the divine essence *Ehyeh* <note>Hebrew: אהיה, meaning "I Am."</note>, from which Plato in his Greek language made this word *on* <note>Greek: ὤν, meaning "the being" or "that which is."</note>, in English "the being" or "the existing"; thus some call God "the Being," and others "the Existing One." There is another name, namely *Hu* <note>Hebrew: הוא, meaning "He."</note>, revealed to Isaiah, which signifies the abyss of divinity, which the Greeks have inter-

Several other names of God and of angels are further derived from the Holy Scriptures by the various Kabbalistic arts: calculatory <term>Gematria: the study of the numerical value of letters</term>, notarial <term>Notarikon: creating acronyms or expanding letters into phrases</term>, and "gimetrian." When they form a name, or several dictions drawn out by certain of their letters, or when a name dispersed by each of its letters signifies or provides several others, it is sometimes drawn from the beginning of the dictions. For example, the name *Agla* <note>Hebrew: אגלא</note> is drawn from this verse of the Holy Scripture: *Atah Gibor Le-olam Adonai* <note>Hebrew: אתה גיבר לעולם אדנו</note>, which is to say, "Thou art the mighty God for eternity." Likewise the name *Iaia* <note>Hebrew: יאיי</note>, drawn from this verse: *Adonai Eloheinu Adonai Echad* <note>Hebrew: יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד</note>, that is to say, "The Lord our God is one single Lord." Similarly, the name *Iava* <note>Hebrew: יואו</note>, drawn from this verse: *Yehi Or Yehi Or* <note>Hebrew: יהי אור יהי אור</note>, that is to say, "Let there be light, and the light was made." Likewise the name *Araritha* <note>Hebrew: אראריתא</note>, taken from this verse of Scripture which carries in English a principle of his unity, a principle of his singularity, his permutation, one thing: *Achad Rosh Achduto Rosh Yichudo Temurato Achad* <note>Hebrew: אחד ראש אחדותו ראש ייחודו תמורתו אחד</note>. There is also another name *Hacaba* <note>Hebrew: הקבא</note>, drawn from this verse: *Ha-Kadosh Barukh Hu* <note>Hebrew: הקדוש ברוך הוא</note>, that is to say in Latin, *sanctus benedictus ipse*, in English, "The Holy One, Blessed be He."

# PHILOSOPHY

Likewise, the name Jesus <note>Hebrew: ישו (*Jesu*)</note> is found at the head of these two verses, namely: *Until Shiloh comes* <note>Hebrew: יבא שילה ולו (*Yavo Shilo V'lo*); original Latin: *quo usque veniat Messia*</note>, that is to say, "until the coming of the Messiah"; and in the other: *His name shall endure* <note>Hebrew: ינון שמו וית (*Yinon Shemo Veyat*); original Latin: *permanet nomen ejus*</note>, that is to say, "his name remains forever." Similarly, this name Amen <note>Hebrew: אמן</note> is drawn from this verse: *The Lord is a faithful King* <note>Hebrew: אדני מלך נאמן (*Adonai Melekh Ne'eman*); original Latin: *Dominus Rex fidelis*</note>. Sometimes these sorts of names are drawn from the ends of words, such as the same name Amen from the end of this verse: *The wicked are not so* <note>Hebrew: לא כן הרשעים (*Lo khen ha-resha'im*); original Latin: *non sic impii*</note>, meaning "it is not thus for the impious"; but by transposing the letters of Amen into the endings of this verse: *To me, what is his name?* <note>Hebrew: לי מה שמו מה (*Li mah shemo mah*); original Latin: *mihi quid... nomen ejus quid*</note>, which carries the sense "to me, what?"; "his name is the 'what'"; one finds the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</term>, which means the "name of four letters."

In the construction of all these names, a letter stands for a word, and the letter is taken from the word—either from the beginning, the end, or from whatever place one wishes—and sometimes these names are drawn from every letter in particular. This is the manner in which those seventy-two names of God are drawn from those three verses of Exodus which begin with these three words: *And he moved*, *And he came*, and *And he stretched out* <note>Hebrew: ויסע ויבא ויט (*Vayissa, Vayavo, Vayete*); these refer to Exodus 14:19-21, where each verse contains exactly 72 letters</note>. The first and last verses are written consecutively from right to left, as we shall demonstrate in what follows. Thus, sometimes one word is drawn from another word, or one name from another name, by the transposition of letters, such as Messiah <note>Hebrew: משיח (*Mashiach*)</note> from *Lishma* <note>Hebrew: לשמה, meaning "for its own sake"</note>; and Michael <note>Hebrew: מיכאל</note> from *Malachi* <note>Hebrew: מאלאכי, meaning "my messenger"</note>. But they are also sometimes formed by a change of alphabet, which the Kabbalists call *Ziruph* <term>Ziruph: a method of permuting or substituting letters using various cipher alphabets</term>, such as from the name Tetragrammaton (the "name of four letters"), YHWH <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note>. From this they derive the names *Mazpaz* <note>Hebrew: מצפצ; a transformation of the name YHWH using a specific substitution cipher</note>.

### OCCULT PHILOSOPHY, Book III.

-> Mazpaz <note>Hebrew: מץפץ (*Matzpaz*), a name derived by substituting letters of the Tetragrammaton</note>, Kuzu <note>Hebrew: כוזו, another substitution for the name of God</note> <-

Sometimes names are also changed by means of numerical equality <term>Gematria: a Kabbalistic method where words are substituted for others with the same numerical value based on their Hebrew letters</term>, such as Metattron <note>Hebrew: מטטרון (*Metatron*), often identified as the highest of angels</note> for Sadai <note>Hebrew: שדי (*Shaddai*), meaning Almighty</note>; for both equal three hundred and fourteen. For the same reason, the name Iiai <note>Hebrew: יאי</note> is equivalent to the name El <note>Hebrew: אל</note> by numerical equality, for both equal thirty-one.

But these are deeply hidden secrets, and it is very difficult to pass judgment on them or to provide a complete science of them; they cannot be understood or taught in any language other than Hebrew. But because the names of God—as Plato says in the *Cratylus* <note>A dialogue concerning the origin of language and whether names are natural or conventional</note>—are in the possession of the Barbarians <note>original: *Barbares*; here referring to the ancient non-Greek peoples, specifically the Hebrews, who were believed to have received the original divine language</note>, who received them from God (without whose assistance no one can in any way understand the words and the true names by which God is called), that is why we can say of them only what God has revealed to us through His pure goodness.

For they are the sacraments and the vehicles of divine power, instituted not by men, nor by angels, but by the great God Himself in a certain manner, according to the immutable number of their characters and their eternal stability. They represent the harmony of the divinity and are sanctified by divine power. This is why the celestial powers fear these names of God, the hells tremble, the angels adore them, the wicked are terrified by them, all creatures revere them, and all religions hold them in veneration.

The religious observance and the pious invocation we make of them with fear and trembling grant us great strength and virtue; they divinize us <note>original: *nous divinisent*; to be made more like God or brought into a state of divine grace</note>, uniting us to God, and also give us the power to perform works and miraculous effects beyond nature. This is why it is permitted to no one whomsoever to ever change them in any manner, nor for any reason whatsoever. It is—

## PHILOSOPHY

...is why Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD) known for his work on biblical interpretation</note> commands that they be kept inviolably in their original characters. Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet to whom many "Chaldean" or magical oracles were attributed in the Renaissance</note> also forbids changing "Barbarian" <note>original: *Barbares*; in this context, referring to non-Greek languages like Hebrew or Egyptian, which were believed to hold more primordial power</note> and Ancient words: For as Plato says in the *Cratylus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the origin of names and language</note>, all divine verbs or names have been communicated to us either by the gods, or by antiquity (whose beginnings are not easy to trace), or we have received them from the Barbarians. Similarly, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and divine mysteries</note> says that one must not pull them from their original languages to put them into another: For, he says, names translated into another language no longer hold the same meaning; consequently, these sacred names of God are a most proper and powerful means for reconciling and uniting man with the gods, as we read in Exodus:
> In every place where you remember my name, I will come to you, and I will bless you. <note>original: Exodus 20:24</note>

The Lord says in the book of Numbers:
> Let them put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will give them my blessing. <note>original: Numbers 6:27</note>

This is why the divine Plato, in the *Cratylus* and the *Philebus*, commands that one should have more respect for divine names than for temples and divine statues, because the image and power of God is more fully formed in the operations of the spirit <note>or mind</note>—principally when it is inspired by God—than in that which is reserved for the works of hands. Therefore, sacred words do not currently possess power in themselves, as words alone in the mouths of Magicians, but they have it through the occult and secret power of the divinities, which operates through their virtue in the spirits of those who have attached themselves to it by faith or secret virtue. God, through these divine names as if by vehicles <term>Vehicles: Here meaning a medium or "vessel" that carries divine influence from the spiritual realm into the material world</term>, is transferred into those who have ears to hear Him, who have become the temple and dwelling place of God, and are purified by the merit of faith and by a great purity of conduct.

# C H A P T E R XIII.

## *Of the members of God, and of their flowing upon ours.*

WE find various passages of Holy Scripture where mention is made of the members and ornaments of God; now, by the members of God, we understand certain forces of several kinds residing permanently in God himself in the greatest simplicity, distinguished by the sacred names of God. The <term>investitures</term> <note>Formal garments or symbols of office; here referring to the ways God clothes His essence to interact with the world.</note> and ornaments of God are like certain ways or relations, emanations, flows, or channels through which he communicates and pours out his benefits upon his creatures. Every time that our soul touches the edges of his garments and ornaments, it will cause to come forth upon itself a divine power from one of the members of God; and the Lord declared this quite clearly regarding the <term>hemorrhaging woman</term> <note>original: "hemorroïsse." Refers to the woman in the Gospels (Luke 8:43-48) who was healed by touching the hem of Jesus's cloak.</note> by saying: "someone touched me, for I felt a power go out from me." Therefore, these members in God are similar to ours, but they are the ideas and the archetypes upon which ours were formed; if we make our members conform, as we ought, to these archetypes, then being changed into the same image, we become the children of God and similar to God, acting and performing the works of God.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### *On the Gods of the heathens, and the souls of celestial bodies, and which places were anciently consecrated to each deity.*

THE PHILOSOPHERS have left us theses which maintain, as we have proven previously, that the Heavens and the Stars are divine animals and that their souls are endowed with understanding, and that they partake of the divine spirit. They have also affirmed that there are other souls which preside over them, and that there are other separate substances above them which act as governors and are commissioned for ministry, which are called intelligences and demons <note>In this context, "demons" refers to the Classical Greek *daimones*—intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses—rather than the malevolent beings of later Christian tradition.</note>. Furthermore, Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose ideas deeply influenced Renaissance magic.</note> himself said that the Celestial souls are not restrained within their bodies as our souls are in ours, but that wherever they wish, they have the joy of seeing God; and that without pain or anxiety they govern their bodies and give them motion, and that simultaneously, through this movement, they govern the things of this lower world without difficulty. This is why it was said that these souls were Gods, and divine honors and prayers were decreed to them, and sacrifices were established for them, and they were honored with various kinds of cults and religions. These are the Gods that all nations have recognized; it is concerning them that Moses made an ordinance in Deuteronomy, contained in these words: lest hav-

### CHAPTER XV.

*Concerning the opinion of our Theologians regarding the celestial souls.*

It is therefore the sentiment not only of the Poets and the Philosophers, but even the Holy Scriptures and the Catholics assure us that the heavens and the celestial bodies are animated by certain divine souls that govern them; for Ecclesiastes <note>Likely referring to the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, traditionally attributed to King Solomon; the text suggests the motions of the sun and wind imply a living agency.</note> himself gives us a description of the soul of heaven; and St. Jerome <note>Original: "St. Hierôme." A prominent 4th-century Church Father known for his Latin translation of the Bible (the Vulgate).</note> in his Commentary on the same expressly confesses and acknowledges it. Origen <note>A 3rd-century theologian whose work *De Principiis* (On First Principles) explored the nature of the soul and the cosmos.</note> similarly in his book *On Principles*, gives us a description of the celestial bodies as being animated and having the absolute use of senses, because they are considered to receive commands from God, which can only befit a rational creature; for it is written, "I have charged all the stars with my command" <note>A reference to Isaiah 45:12.</note>: and one even notices that Job agreed that the stars were not entirely exempt from the stain of sin; for here is what we read there: "the stars likewise are not pure in his presence" <note>Job 25:5. The French text uses "mondes," an archaic form of the word for "pure" or "clean."</note>; which cannot truly refer to their physical brightness.

The celestial bodies thus have their souls; this is also the sentiment of Eusebius Pamphilius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian church.</note> in his *Theological Solutions*; and of St. Augustine in his *Enchi-*

# CHAPTER XVI.

## *Concerning intelligences and demons, their three different types, and their various surnames; together with infernal and subterranean demons.*

Now, following the order and connection of the subjects, we must speak here of intelligences, spirits, and demons. An intelligence is a thinking substance, free from any mass of dense and corruptible body, immortal, functioning without the use of senses, present everywhere, and capable of acting upon all things; and all intelligences, spirits, and <term>demons<note>Original: "demons." The author is using the term in the classical Greek sense of *daimon*, meaning a spirit or divine power, rather than the modern sense of an evil "devil."</note></term> are of the same nature. Now, I call them "demons" here—not those whom we commonly call devils, but spirits named according to the proper meaning of the word, as one might say "learned," "intelligent," and "wise." According to what the <term>Magicians<note>Original: "Magiciens." Practitioners of "High Magic" or "Natural Magic" who studied the hidden laws of the universe and the spiritual hierarchies.</note></term> teach us, there are three types of these spirits. 

Those of the first order they call <term>supercelestial<note>Original: "surcelestes." Spirits that exist above or beyond the physical heavens and the planetary spheres.</note></term>, being souls entirely separated from the body—almost like intellectual spheres that adore and serve the one God. He is their unity, or the firm and stable center to which they all relate; for this reason, they call them "gods" from that point on, because they participate in some way in the divinity, being always filled with God and quenched by the divine <term>nectar<note>Original: "nectar." A metaphorical reference to divine grace or wisdom, drawing on classical mythology where nectar was the drink of the gods.</note></term>. They are occupied near God

This is the belief of the **Egyptians** and the **Platonists**, which **Proclus** principally maintains alongside them; as do **Plutarch**, **Demetrius** the Philosopher, and **Aemilianus** the Rhetorician, who all assert the same thing. For they bear this public testimony: that among the wonders of their time, **Pan**, the great spirit, and several others, had cried out loudly while weeping, and that they had also died after these cries.

It is said then, according to the opinion of the Platonists, that there are as many legions of demons of this third kind as there are stars in the sky, and that there are as many demons in each legion as the heaven itself contains stars. ->## PHILOSOPHY<-

**Athanasius** has left it in writing that, in proportion to the number of men, there are 99 parts <note>Athanasius likely refers here to the heavenly host, following the interpretation of the Parable of the Lost Sheep where the 99 who did not go astray represent the angels, and the one lost sheep represents humanity.</note>, according to the parable of the hundred sheep; others raise it to nine parts only, following the parable of the ten drachmas; others estimate that the number of angels is equal to that of men, seeing as it is written: *He set the bounds of the people according to the number of the angels of God.* <note>Originally a reference to Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Septuagint translation.</note> Many other authors have written several other things concerning the number of angels; but the most recent theologians after the <term>Master of the Sentences<note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1164), whose *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note></term>, **Augustine**, and **Gregory** easily extricate themselves from this difficulty by saying that the number of good angels exceeds the comprehension of all men, and that there is, on the contrary, an infinite number of unclean spirits who inhabit this lower world, and that there are pure spirits in the superior world. According to the testimony of some theologians who claim to have learned it through oracles, they place among the number of these wicked ones the genre of subterranean or shadowy demons, whom the <term>Platonists<note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato.</note></term> call the "deserting angels," avengers of crimes and impieties, according to the decree of divine justice.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *Concerning the same angels according to the opinions of the Theologians.*

As for our theologians, being of one mind with **Saint Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian whose work *The Celestial Hierarchy* became the definitive guide for angelic categorization.</note>, they identify three distinctions of angels, each of which they divide into three orders, thus creating three distinctions and nine orders in total. They call these orders <term>Hierarchies<note>From the Greek *hierarchia*, meaning "holy rule" or "sacred order."</note></term> and the distinctions <term>Choirs<note>Groups of angels singing or acting in unison around the divine throne.</note></term>. **Proclus** <note>Proclus Lycaeus (412–485 AD), a Greek Neoplatonist whose philosophical frameworks deeply influenced early Christian angelology.</note> also divides them by the number nine.

In the first Hierarchy, they place the **Seraphim**, the **Cherubim**, and the **Thrones**, considering them to be the <term>supercelestial spirits<note>Spirits existing above the physical heavens, in the realm of pure divine thought.</note></term> or demons who contemplate the order of God’s providence: the first in His goodness, the second in His essence as form, and the third in His wisdom. In the second Hierarchy, they place the **Dominations**,

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### *Of the orders of evil demons, of their fall, and of their various natures.*

There are some theological doctors who likewise establish nine classes of evil demons, as many adversary troops opposed to the nine orders of angels. The first class of these wicked spirits are the <term>Pseudotheoi</term> <note>from the Greek *pseudos* (false) and *theos* (god)</note>, that is to say, the false Gods; they are so named because they usurp the name of God and wish to be worshipped as Gods. They demand sacrifices and adorations, like that demon who said to Jesus Christ in the Gospel, "If you worship me by prostrating yourself on the ground, I will give you all that you see," while showing him all the Kingdoms of the earth. Their Prince is he who says, "I will rise above the heights of the clouds and I will be like the Most High." For this reason, he is called <term>Beelzebub</term> <note>original: *Belzebut*; the author interprets this name here as "Old God," though it is more commonly translated from Hebrew/Philistine as "Lord of the Flies."</note>, that is to say, "old God." After these are the spirits of lying, such as was that spirit of lying that appeared before the prophets of **Ahab** <note>A biblical reference to 1 Kings 22:22, where a spirit volunteers to be a "lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" to lead the King of Israel to his downfall.</note>; and their prince is that famous serpent <term>Python</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the Python was a monstrous serpent slain by Apollo; the author here links this pagan figure to the hierarchy of fallen spirits.</note> who gave the name "Pythian" to Apollo.

# PHILOSOPHY

[Augus]tine <note>The text completes the name of Saint Augustine from the previous page</note> in the first book of *The Incarnation of the Word* addressed to Januarius, where he likewise says regarding the Devil and his angels, those enemies of virtues: the Church has taught in its preaching that they are truly in this lower world, but it has not determined clearly enough who they are, nor in what manner they exist. 

Here, however, is the opinion that many authors hold regarding these kinds of spirits: that this Devil was once a good angel, but he became an **apostate** <term>Apostate: Someone who abandons their religious faith or divine service</term> by leaving the service of God, and that he persuaded several other angels to join him in leaving God’s side, causing their fall. To this day, these are still called "his angels." 

Nevertheless, the Greek Church does not deny that all these spirits are damned, but suggests that they are not all wicked by deliberate purpose. Instead, they believe that since the creation of the world, the disposition of things was ordained such that these malevolent spirits would serve as the "executioners" of sinful souls. 

Other theologians say that God did not create evil demons at all; rather, they were drawn from the ranks of the good angels and were chased and cast out of heaven because of their **prevarication** <term>Prevarication: In this context, a transgression or a straying from the path of divine truth</term>. Not only do our theologians and those of the Hebrews teach us this, but the Assyrians, Arabs, Egyptians, and Greeks all confirm the fall of these miserable spirits through their own doctrines. 

Pherecydes of Syros <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek philosopher often credited with being among the first to write on the immortality of the soul</note> gives us a description of the fall of the demons, and says that **Ophis**—that is to say, the demonic serpent <note>original: *Ophis*, from the Greek word for serpent, ὄφις</note>—commands this army of spirits revolted against God. This same fall is reported to us by Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pimandre* <note>The *Poimandres*, the first and most famous text of the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note>, and by Homer, who published it in his verses. Plutarch, in his discourse on usury, gives us to understand that Empedocles <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed the four-element theory of the universe</note> had knowledge of this fall of the demons. The demons themselves have confessed the misfortune of their fall on several occasions...

In this way, through that subsequent penance, and by following the same path after the resurrection that they had taken to assume human flesh, they might have been able to return from their exile to the vision of God. They would then be delivered from their ethereal and aerial bodies, and in this state, all the powers of heaven, earth, and hell would have bowed their knees prostrate before God, so that "God may be all in all." According to the history of **Paul the Hermit** <note>Paul of Thebes, considered the first Christian hermit</note>, written by **St. Jerome** and revered in the canonical hours throughout the Church, and also according to the legend of **Brendan** <note>Saint Brendan the Navigator, an Irish monk famous for his legendary voyage across the Atlantic</note>, they were thus informed, and they maintain that their prayers will be heard, for this reason alone: that we read in the Gospel that Jesus Christ granted the prayer of the demons, and permitted them to enter into the herd of swine. ## CHAPTER XIX.

### *Concerning the bodies of demons.*

MODERN theologians and philosophers are in great disagreement regarding the bodies of demons; for **St. Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a dominant figure in Scholasticism who argued that angels and demons are entirely incorporeal</note> asserts that all angels have no bodies, nor do evil spirits; but that they sometimes take on bodies which they discard shortly thereafter. And **St. Denis** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose work *The Divine Names* was a foundational text for Christian angelology</note> says consistently in *The Divine Names* that angels have no bodies; nevertheless, **St. Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</note>, in his commentary on Genesis, expresses himself thus on this matter: "Demons are considered creatures of air and fire, because they are vigorous by means of the nature of aerial bodies, and do not perish by death, because the element is more suited in them for acting than for suffering." <note>In the physics of the time, "acting" referred to the ability to exert force, while "suffering" (or passion) referred to the capacity to be changed or harmed by external forces</note> The same St. Augustine seems to establish that, as for the angels, they had from the beginning of their creation bodies of air formed from the purest and highest portion of the air, fit for acting and not for suffering; and that after their confirmation <note>Theological term for the state of grace in which good angels were permanently fixed after their initial choice to serve God</note>, this nature was preserved for the good angels, but it was changed for the wicked ones during their fall into the quality of the coarsest air, so that they may even be tormented by fire. Furthermore, the great **St. Basil** <note>Basil of Caesarea (330–379 AD), one of the Cappadocian Fathers</note> gives not only to demons, but also to pure angels likewise, bodies which are like certain subtle aerial and pure spirits. **St. Gregory of Nazianzus** is also of the opinion of these Fathers. **Apuleius** <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), a Platonist philosopher whose writings on "daemons" as intermediary beings between gods and men were influential</note> believes that the angels do not have

But Sillas <note>Likely a reference to Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine philosopher and Christian who wrote extensively on the classification and physical nature of demons in *De Operatione Daemonum*.</note>, a disciple of Plato and a Christian, does not believe that the nature of demons is without a body; nevertheless, the body of the angel is not the same thing as the body of the demon. For the angel's body is exempt from all matter, but the demon's body is made of some matter, like the bodies of shadows, and is subject to suffering <note>In this context, "suffering" refers to the philosophical concept of *passio*, meaning the capacity to be acted upon or to experience external sensations, including pain.</note>, so that it feels pain when struck, and fire changes it into visible ashes—which is said to have occurred in the past in Tuscany. And although the body of the demon is spiritual, it is nonetheless highly sensitive and suffers at the touch; and even though it may be cut, it rejoins and remakes itself like air and water, yet it suffers great pain. This is why demons fear the edge of a blade, arrows, and swords; from this it follows that in Virgil, the Sibyl has Aeneas put his sword in hand, saying to him:
> Seize the path, and draw your sword from its scabbard. <note>original: "saisissez vous du passage, & tiré vôtre épée du foureau." This is a translation of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, 260: "tuque invade viam vaginaque eripe ferrum."</note>

Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note>, explaining this passage, says that Aeneas wanted to have a consecrated sword. Orpheus also describes these sorts of demoniac bodies; there is truly a kind of body that is composed only of fire, but which is invisible, and it is these that Orpheus calls <term>igneous demons</term> and <term>celestial</term> <note>These were thought to inhabit the highest, purest regions of the heavens.</note>. There is a second kind composed of fire and air mixed and matched equally, which makes the <term>ethereal demons</term> and <term>aerial demons</term>. And if there entered into the composition of this kind of body some portion of water, there results a third difference of body from which come the <term>water demons</term>, who are sometimes seen; if one adds to them something earthly that is not coarse, they are called

One does not need to pay as much heed to the other demons; they are not so troublesome, nor always invisible; they appear sometimes and change into different figures. They also take on forms made of shadows, of funerary likenesses, laden with a grime and a moisture of fatty bodies; and they have an excessive communication with the matter called by the Ancients the *malignant soul* <note>original: "ame maligne". It is written concerning John the Baptist in Malachi: "Behold, I send my angel before your face." <note>Malachi 3:1. The author uses this to show that "angel" can refer to a messenger or a spiritual guide.</note> It is written elsewhere of this change and union in these terms: "He who attaches himself to God becomes one spirit with God." <note>1 Corinthians 6:17.</note> Similarly, the evil spirit works to make us like him and attached to him by means of the evil deeds into which he draws us, as Jesus Christ says concerning Judas in these words: "Have I not chosen you twelve, and yet one of you is a devil?" <note>John 6:70.</note> And this is what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Greek-Egyptian figure to whom a vast body of mystical and alchemical writings (the Hermetica) was attributed.</note> says: "When the devil slips into a soul, he sows the seeds of his own knowledge," which causes such a soul, burdened with these evil seeds and filled with fury, to perform surprising things by this means, and all the tricks that demons do. And the good spirit, on the contrary, when it enters a holy soul, raises it to the light of wisdom. But the wicked spirit, having slid into a soul, carries it toward thefts, homicides, debaucheries <term>paillardises|A term encompassing various forms of lewdness or carnal sin.</term>, and all sorts of diabolical occupations. The good angels, says Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who focused on theurgy, the practice of rituals intended to bring the practitioner into contact with the divine.</note>, push souls toward the ultimate purity; others bestow even more benefits upon us. They grant us, through their presence, the health of the body, the strength of the mind, and the security of the soul; they remove what is mortal, preserve our natural heat, and make it stronger to sustain life, always enlightening man through the harmony they create between the understanding and the spirit.

Theologians dispute whether man has several guardian angels, or if he has only one? For our part, we believe that he has several, according to the words of the Prophet: "He has given his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways." <note>Psalm 91:11.</note> This is understood, according to the testimony of St. Jerome <note>An early Christian priest and scholar (c. 342–420 AD), best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>, not only regarding Jesus Christ, but also regarding every individual man. # OCCULT PHILOSOPHY, Book III #

[These souls] are therefore governed by the ministry of various spirits, and are led each to every degree of virtue, merit, and dignity, provided they have made themselves worthy of them and of their good offices. On the contrary, the unworthy are cast down by the wicked spirits, and at the same time by the good ones as well, and pushed to the final degree of misery according to the requirements of their demerits. All those who are guarded by more sublime angels are above other men; for their angels, who take care of them, elevate them and subject others to them by a certain secret force. Although no one perceives it, he nevertheless feels a certain yoke of precedence <term>preséance|The right to precede others in rank or importance; a natural sense of hierarchy.</term> from which he cannot easily discharge himself; on the contrary, he fears and reveres this force and power that the superior angels send to their superiors, and they engage the inferiors through a certain terror that makes them fear this precedence.

It seems that Homer was of this sentiment in the passage where he says that the Muses, daughters of Jupiter, are always inseparable companions in the presence of Kings, who are also sons of Jupiter, and that their presence makes them venerable and majestic. We read similarly that when Marc Antony <note>Marcus Antonius (83–30 BC), the Roman general and member of the Second Triumvirate.</note> had become a great friend of Octavian Augustus <note>Gaius Octavius, the future first Roman Emperor Augustus. The rivalry between Antony and Octavian is a cornerstone of Roman history.</note>, they often used to play together, but Augustus always won. ## CHAPTER XXII.

*That every man has three guardian angels, or genii; and from where each of these three genii comes to us.*

THERE is no man on earth who does not have around him for his own protection [three spirits]: the first is sacred, the second comes from birth, and the third is for one's profession: the sacred spirit <term>sacred spirit: Often referred to in occult philosophy as the "Sacred Guardian Angel," a divine spark that transcends physical nature.</term> according to the doctrine of the Egyptians <note>Early modern occultists frequently attributed their ideas to "Egyptian" wisdom, specifically the Hermetic tradition, which they believed predated Greek philosophy.</note> does not come from the stars nor the planets; but it comes from a superior power—the master of spirits, who is God himself—who gave it to the soul as it left his hands to descend from heaven to earth. This spirit is universal and above nature: it is he who is the director of the soul’s life, and who always presents good thoughts to the mind, acting within us incessantly and communicating to us the lights of salvation, even though we do not always pay attention. But when we are washed of our sins, and lead a tranquil life, then we recognize him; he almost converses with us, and makes us hear his voice, although previously he kept silence in our presence, and he strives without ceasing to make us reach the perfection of the saints. ## CHAPTER XXIV.

### *Concerning the names of spirits and their various assignments: furthermore, of the spirits who preside over the stars, the poles of heaven, and the Elements.*

THE **NAMES** of spirits, both good and evil, are of many kinds and very different; their proper and true names, just like those of all others, are known only to **God** alone, who alone can count the multitude of the stars and call them by their names <note>A reference to Psalm 147:4: "He determines the number of the stars and calls them each by name."</note>; we cannot know any of them unless God reveals them to us, and we find very few of them stated in the **Holy Scriptures**. However, the **Hebrew doctors** believe that **Adam** gave names to the spirits, just as this passage of Scripture says: *God brought before Adam all that He had made, so that he might give each of them their names, and the name he gave to each thing is its true name.* <note>Referencing Genesis 2:19. In the occult tradition, this "naming" is seen as a divine act of defining the essence and power of a being.</note> On this foundation, the <term>Mecubales</term> <note>From the Hebrew *Mekubbalim*, meaning "receivers"; a term used for practitioners of the Kabbalah who receive oral tradition.</note> of the **Hebrews** believe that man can also give names to the spirits, but only he who has previously rendered himself worthy, and who, by a very particular gift from God or a sacred power, has been elevated to this virtue. I have personally seen and known a certain individual who wrote the name and the sign <note>Often referred to as a "sigil," a unique symbol representing a specific spirit.</note> of a certain spirit on virgin parchment <note>Parchment made from the skin of an animal that had not yet mated, considered "pure" for ritual use.</note> during the hour of the Moon <note>In traditional astrology, each hour of the day is governed by a specific planet; the "hour of the Moon" was thought best for magic involving water or transformation.</note>. Of this sort are the names of the angels that follow: **Raziel**, **Gabriel**, **Michael**, **Raphael**, and **Haniel**, which signify *vision of God*, *virtue of God*, *strength of God*, and *medicine of God* <note>original: "vision de Dieu, vertu de Dieu, force de Dieu, medicine de Dieu"</note>. ## CHAPTER XXV.

->*How the Hebrew Doctors <note>A term used by Renaissance scholars to refer to Rabbis and Kabbalists.</note> derive the sacred names of the Angels from the Holy Scriptures; and concerning the 72 Angels who bear the name of God; as well as the Ziruph tables <note>original: "tables Ziruph." From the Hebrew 'Tziruf,' meaning the art of combining and permuting letters to find hidden meanings or names.</note>, and the change they make of letters and numbers.*<-

There are yet other sacred names of both good and evil spirits, assigned to each of their offices, far more powerful than those we have spoken of before, which are drawn from the Holy Scriptures, according to the art taught by the Hebrew Kabbalists <term>Mecubales: From the Hebrew 'Mekubbalim,' meaning those who have received the secret tradition or Kabbalah.</term>; just as certain names of God are also drawn from certain passages of the Scriptures. Their general rule is that wherever something concerning the divine essence is expressed in the Holy Scriptures, a name of God can be systematically derived from that place. And wherever a name of God is found expressed in the holy letters, one may judge from there the office that corresponds to that name. Consequently, in every place where the Scripture speaks of the ministry or the work of any good or evil spirit, one can derive the name of the good or evil spirit from that place. Let us therefore observe, inviolably and without changing anything, this method or general rule, which requires us to derive the names of the good spirits from the

## VOLUME II. ANOTHER CIRCULAR TABLE CALLED IRRATIONAL. PAGE 109 IV.

### SECOND TABLE
<note>original: "TABULA SECUNDA"</note>

<term>Tabula Recta|A cryptographic tool consisting of a square grid where each row is a version of the alphabet shifted one position to the left. It is the foundation of polyalphabetic ciphers, allowing a single letter to be represented by many different cipher-letters depending on its position in the text.</term>

The following table is an "Irrational" grid. Unlike a standard alphabet, it uses a specific 24-character sequence: **m c r i n m u r a c t o v e z c r u n m u r a c**. This sequence is rotated across 22 rows to create a complex field for encoding. 

<note>This specific sequence does not form a standard word in Latin or French, suggesting it may be a "key" or a phonetic representation of a Hebrew phrase used in Kabbalistic practice. The handwritten marks superimposed on the printed grid suggest that a later scholar or practitioner was using this table to decode a specific hidden message.</note>

<note>This table is a classic example of Renaissance <term>cryptography|the practice of secure communication</term> as described by authors like Trithemius. The use of <term>combinatorics|the study of permutations and arrangements</term> allows for a massive number of potential secret keys. ## CHAPTER XXVI.

*How to derive the names of spirits and geniuses from the arrangement of the celestial bodies.*

The ancient Magicians have given us the art of finding the name of the spirit that one must invoke to produce a desired effect, by deriving it from the arrangement of the heavens. For example, they propose a certain celestial harmony <note>The concept of "musica universalis" or the music of the spheres, where the movements of celestial bodies are seen as mathematical proportions or "harmony."</note> to create an image, or a ring, or some other work, in order to find—under a specific constellation—the guiding spirit of that work. Having drawn a figure of the heavens <note>A horoscope or astrological chart showing the positions of the planets and signs at a specific moment.</note>, one distributes the letters [of the alphabet] by their number and order starting from the degree of the ascendant <note>The <term>ascendant</term> is the degree of the zodiac that is rising on the eastern horizon at the time of the chart.</note>, following the sequence of the signs through every degree until the entire circuit of the sky is filled. Then, this circle of the same letters—which have fallen into place by casting them upon the locations of the stars—are looked upon as the presiding forces. These are marked and written separately from the figure in that same number and order; according to the number and powers of these stars, they form and designate the name of the spirit—specifically, the good spirit. But if you do this starting from the first degree of the west <note>The Descendant, or the point directly opposite the Ascendant.</note> against the progress and order of the signs, the spirit signified by the letters will be one of the evil ones.

Certain Hebrew and Chaldean masters teach how to seek the nature and the <term>genius</term> <note>In this context, a "genius" is a tutelary or guardian spirit assigned to a person, place, or object from birth or creation.</note> of every man through this artifice, which is, that having

# CHAPTER XXVII.

## *Of the art of calculating these kinds of names according to the tradition of the Cabalists.*

There is yet another device for the invention of these types of names which is called calculatory <note>This refers to an algorithmic or mathematical method of rearranging letters to find hidden meanings.</note>, and it is performed by the following tables, entering with some great or sacred name of God, or of angels, into the column of descending letters, and taking the letters that you find in the common angles beneath their stars; and having arranged them in order, they form the name of the good spirit of the nature of the star, or of the sign, under which you have entered. And if you enter the ascending column by taking the common angles above the stars and signs marked on the bottom line, the name of the evil spirit is found made. And behold, these are the names of the spirits, both good and evil, assigned from all the orders or parts of the heaven to their offices, which you can multiply in this way into nine names, as many as there are orders in this table. That is to say, by entering with one name, you can derive from that name another name of a spirit of a higher order, whether good or evil; nevertheless, the principle of calculation depends upon the names of God: for every voice has power in Magic, in that it depends upon the voice of God, and that it is formed [by it].

<note>This table is a permutation grid used in Kabbalistic magic. By finding the intersection of a specific letter (representing a name or intention) and a Zodiac sign, the practitioner "extracts" a new letter. This sequence of extracted letters forms the name of a spirit or "genie" associated with that astrological influence. The "Entrance of the Good" likely refers to the calculation of benevolent spirits (angels), while the "Entrance of the Wicked" refers to the calculation of malevolent ones (demons).</note>

It is used to derive the names of spiritual entities by intersecting linguistic "entrances" with celestial positions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the cryptographic systems of Johannes Trithemius, likely from his work "Steganographia." While the previous page utilized the Hebrew alphabet to map celestial correspondences, Table II shifts to the Greek alphabet. These tables were designed to appear as mystical tools for summoning angels, but they functioned as "tabula combinatoria"—substitution ciphers where specific letters from a hidden message would be replaced by those in the table to create a seemingly pious prayer.</meta>

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

->*How the names of spirits are sometimes taken from the very things over which they preside.*<-

I find yet another kind of names taken from the things themselves that have angels as their presiding rulers; these are imposed upon them as if they borrowed a name from the stars, or from men, or from places, or from times, or from similar things, adding a name of God at the end to form it <note>Specifically the suffix "-el," which means "of God"</note>. In this manner, the spirit of Saturn is called Sabathiel <note>Derived from *Shabbathai*, the Hebrew name for Saturn</note>; the spirit of Jupiter, Zedekiel <note>Derived from *Tzedek*, meaning Justice, the Hebrew name for Jupiter</note>; the spirit of Mars, Madimiel <note>Derived from *Ma'adim*, the Hebrew name for Mars</note>; the spirit of the Sun, Semiliel Semeschiap <note>Derived from *Shemesh*, the Hebrew word for the Sun</note>; the spirit of Venus, Nogahel <note>Derived from *Nogah*, the Hebrew name for Venus</note>; the spirit of Mer-

## CHAPTER XXXII.

### *How we must attract to ourselves and win over good spirits; and how we can convince the evil ones.*

# CHAPTER XXXIII.

## *On the bonds of spirits, their conjurations, and the manner of banishing them.*

# CHAPTER XXXVI.

## *How man was created in the likeness of God.*

GOD being the sovereign fullness of all goods, as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus: a legendary Hellenistic figure perceived during the Renaissance as an ancient Egyptian prophet and the author of the *Hermetica*, texts which blended philosophy, magic, and theology.</note> says, made two portraits which are similar to him in order to make himself known to men, namely, the world and man. In the first of these, he proposed to make a display of his divine operations, and in the other, to take his pleasures. And because God is one, for that reason he made only one world; and because he is infinite, he made the world round <note>In Renaissance cosmology, the sphere was considered the most "infinite" and perfect shape because it has no beginning or end, mirroring God’s eternal nature.</note>; being eternal, he created the world incorruptible and eternal; being immense, he created the world as the greatest thing; and because he is life itself in its sovereignty, he also enriched the world with vital seeds <term>semences vitales|Based on the Latin *rationes seminales*, these were thought to be spiritual "blueprints" or life-forces implanted by God into the fabric of the universe to allow for the generation of all living things.</term>, capable of producing, and indeed producing, all things from its own depths; and because he alone is the Almighty, he created the world of his pure will, without any necessity of nature, not from a matter that existed before the world, but from pure nothingness <note>original: "pur néant" — This emphasizes the doctrine of *creatio ex nihilo* (creation out of nothing), asserting that God did not require pre-existing "stuff" to build the universe.</note>; and because he is sovereign goodness, by embracing his Word <note>original: "verbe" — Referring to the *Logos*, the divine reason or creative utterance of God.</note>, which is the first of all his ideas, of his good will and with an essential love, he made the external world upon the model of the internal world, which is the ideal world, yet without putting anything of the essence of the Idea outside of himself; rather, he created from nothing in time that which he held by Idea in eternity.

To die is therefore a name that says nothing; and just as the vacuum is nothing positive that has existence, and which holds a place among the beings of nature, so death or dying is a term that signifies nothing real and positive that takes place among the things of nature. We do not say of man, then, that when the soul and the body separate, anything of either perishes or falls back into nothingness.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.

### How the influences from above, being good by their nature, become bad in the things of this low world, and are the cause of evils.

Since all virtue and power come from above, first from God, then from the intelligences, and from the stars in succession—none of which can err nor do evil—it must be that all evils, and everything found here below that is contrary and harmful, come from the ill-disposed nature of the subject that receives them; as Chrysippus <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) who argued that while the universe is governed by providence, human suffering is often a result of our own character.</note> says very well in his poetry in these terms:

> *How wrongly mortals accuse the gods, and complain of them alone; for we ourselves are the cause of our misfortunes, and each person suffers only through their own fault.*
