## CHAPTER XL.
### *That every man carries the mark of God imprinted upon him, by the virtue of which he may succeed in performing miracles.*

IT has been proven by no small experience that man possesses the power to dominate and to halt whomever he wishes, a power which he holds by title of nature alone. For according to the testimony of **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 AD), the Roman author of *Natural History*, whose descriptions of animal behavior were foundational for Renaissance science.</note>, it is said that the elephant quietly shows the way to a man he encounters who has lost his path in the desert. It is also said that this same animal, perceiving the tracks of a man before seeing the man himself, trembles for fear of his snares; he stops, looks about him, and is seized by an extreme dread. Likewise the tiger, more cruel than other wild beasts, upon seeing a man, is said to immediately carry its young elsewhere; and many other similar facts are reported by various Authors who have composed great volumes on the nature of animals. # CHAPTER XLI.

### What is thought concerning man after death, and the various opinions on this matter.

IT IS a statute ordained for all men to die once in their lives, and death is inevitable; but there are several kinds of death. This one happens according to the laws of nature; that one by violent accidents which destroy the nature of man; another is voluntary; and the fourth is ordained by human laws for crimes committed, or sent by God for sin, so that it does not seem that men dying in this way have paid their tribute to nature, but rather have undergone the penalty due to their demerits. It is this penalty, as the Hebrew Doctors <note>Referring to Jewish sages and Kabbalists, whose traditions Agrippa frequently integrates into his work.</note> say, that God never remits to anyone. This is why He gave His conditions to Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechias"; the King of Judah. This refers to a Talmudic tradition (Sanhedrin 37b) suggesting that even when the legal power of the courts to execute criminals was lost, divine providence ensured the punishments were still carried out through "accidents."</note>: that since the house of the sanctuary had been plundered, although no order of judicial execution remained, no one worthy of death had escaped the four types of punishments <note>In Jewish law, these were stoning, burning, beheading, and strangling.</note> to which they were ordinarily condemned, without having suffered other similar penalties. For he who had deserved to be stoned, by God's permission, would throw himself from the top of a house, or be devoured by wild beasts, or remain crushed under some ruin or some fall; he who had deserved fire, was consumed in

### OCCULT [PHILOSOPHY], Book III.

As for the spirit of man, whose nature was holy and whose origin was divine, because it never commits a fault, it is also not subject to punishment. Regarding the soul: if it has done well, it enters into joy with the spirit and, exiting the body with its ethereal vehicle, it ascends freely to the choir of heroes and goes to join the gods. <term>ethereal vehicle: In Neoplatonic philosophy, this was a "star-like" body of light that served as a middle ground between the immaterial soul and the physical body, allowing the soul to travel through the celestial spheres.</term> There, being beatified in all its senses and powers, it enjoys perpetual happiness and a perfect knowledge of all things; furthermore, it enjoys the vision of God and the possession of the kingdom of heaven. Having a share in the power of God, it does good for those it has left on earth; it bestows various gifts and favors upon them like the immortal God.

But if it has done evil, the spirit <note>Agrippa distinguishes here between the "spirit" (the highest, divine spark of reason) and the "soul" (the seat of emotions and personality).</note> judges it and abandons it to the will of the demon. The poor soul, in sadness, abandoned by its spirit, wanders lost in the underworlds in the form of an idol, which is called an image—just as the unfortunate Dido complains in Virgil, saying:

> *And now it is necessary that my image, great as it is,*
> *must go and hide beneath the earth.*
> <note>original: "Et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago." — Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book IV, line 654. Dido says this before her suicide.</note>

Therefore, this soul—no longer possessing its intelligible essence and abandoned to the empire of its fantasy—is likewise subject to the evils of bodily qualities. <term>fantasy: In this historical context, "fantasy" (phantaisie) refers to the lower imaginative faculty that processes sensory images, which becomes a source of torment when the soul loses its higher reasoning power.</term> It knows itself to be deprived for eternity by its own fault and by a just judgment of God from the divine vision. As Scripture testifies, this deprivation of the vision of God is the presence of all evils and is the most cruel punishment of all. The Holy Scriptures call it the pouring out of the wrath of God. Consequently, this image of the soul, sometimes taking a body of air, covers itself with a shadow, and enveloping itself in it—

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "state of the soul after death" from page 188, specifically citing the Church Fathers Augustine and Ambrose to support the idea of an intermediate state—a "waiting room" of sorts—before the final resurrection.</meta>

<header>OCCULT [PHILOSOPHY], Book III.</header>

The same opinion is followed by St. Augustine and St. Ambrose. The former says in his *Manual* <note>original: "Manuel"; referring to Augustine’s *Enchiridion*, a handbook on Christian doctrine</note> that during the time between a person's death and their final resurrection, souls are held in hidden retreats, according to whether they deserve rest or punishment, and according to what they did, well or ill, while living in the body. However, the book *On the Benefit of Death* <note>original: "le livre du bien de la mort"; referencing St. Ambrose’s treatise *De bono mortis*</note> states that the Book of Esdras <note>referring to the apocryphal *Second Book of Esdras* (or 4 Ezra), which was highly regarded by some early theologians</note> calls these dwellings of souls "reservoirs" <note>original: "reſervoirs"; often translated from the Latin *promptuaria* as storehouses or promptuaries</note>. This same book—anticipating the complaint of man that the righteous who have gone before seem to be frustrated by a long delay of the reward due to them by a miracle—says that the day of judgment is like the crown that a brave man deserves. Everyone awaits the day of crowning, so that on that day, confusion may make the defeated blush, and the victors may appear publicly with palms in hand as a mark of their victory. Thus, souls await the fulfillment of the time God has limited and the reward they deserve: some punishment, others glory. In the same chapter of this book, the underworld <note>original: "l'enfer"; here used in the sense of the Latin *infernus* or the Greek *Hades*, meaning the place of the dead generally, not just the place of punishment</note> is called an "invisible place" where souls go once delivered from their bodies. Sometimes the entire soul returns to reason, either seeking certain things through reasoning or by considering itself. Finally, reason has its own empire, which is that whenever something presents itself—whether to the understanding, or to the idol, or to nature, or to a body—it cannot pass into the soul without reason knowing of it. In this way, the soul receives nothing through the external senses—it neither sees, nor hears, nor feels, nor suffers anything—until the **cogitative reason** conceives it beforehand. Now, it conceives it when it is not occupied, and not when it is busy with something else; as we clearly see in those who do not recognize those they meet when they are strongly occupied with something else. # CHAPTER XLVI.

## Of the first kind of fury, proceeding from the Muses.

**FURY** <note>From the Latin *furor*, meaning a state of divine madness or inspired trance</note> is an illumination of the soul proceeding from the gods, or from spirits <note>Original: "demons," which in this Renaissance context refers to *daimons* or intermediary spirits rather than evil entities</note>, from which comes this couplet from Ovid:

> *God is within us, and also commerce with heaven; this spirit comes to us from the celestial dwellings.* <note>A translation of Ovid's *Fasti* VI, 5: "Est deus in nobis, agitante calescimus illo."</note>

Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century and founder of Neoplatonism</note> says that this spirit of prophecy is an alienation and a knot, since it is not found in those whose bodily senses are awake; being opposed to the animal man, it attaches itself to the divinity who gives it those things which it cannot seek out for itself by its own strength. For when the spirit—free and disengaged, letting go of the body's reins as if escaping from a guarded prison—goes out into a greater liberty and unchains itself from the irons of the body's members without hindrance from anyone, then man, being himself driven by the spirit of God, understands all things and foresees future events. There are four species of divine fury proceeding from their respective divinities: namely, from the Muses, from Dionysus <note>Original: "Denis," the French form of Dionysius/Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy</note>, from Apollo, and from Venus.

The sixth degree depends on Jupiter; this degree governs the discourses of reason, deliberations, consultations, and moral resolutions. <note>Original: *absolutions morales*, referring to the process of making definitive moral judgments or settling the mind's intent.</note> These things have been partly discussed below; it also holds under its power wonders and venerations, the astonishment of which sometimes stops the imagination and reason so completely that they suddenly forget all their own actions. The seventh degree represents Saturn; this degree governs the most secret intelligences and the tranquil contemplations of the spirit. I call contemplation here that free clarity of the spirit, fixed with admiration upon the spectacles of wisdom; for that invention of the spirit, which is done through enigmas or images, is a kind of speculation or reasoning that belongs to Jupiter; it is not a contemplation.

The eighth degree, representing the starry heaven <note>The "ciel des étoiles" refers to the Firmament or the sphere of the fixed stars, including the zodiac.</note>, observes the situation, the movement, the rays, and the light of the celestial bodies; it also holds the images, the rings, and similar things that are manufactured according to the rule of celestial things, of which we have spoken previously.

The ninth degree corresponds to the First Mover <note>Original: *premier mobile*. In the geocentric model, this is the outermost sphere that moves all the inner spheres.</note>, namely, to the ninth sphere, or to the universe itself; this degree contains more formal things, such as numbers, figures, and characters, and observes the secret influences of the intelligences of heaven, and raises the rest of the other secrets. RAPTURE is a detachment, a withdrawal, and an illumination of the soul proceeding from God, by which God once again withdraws the soul from the earth where He had sent it from heaven, in order to lift it back to the heaven from which it had descended. The cause of this lifting is a perpetual contemplation that we direct toward the most sublime things; insofar as this contemplation joins us—by a strong intention of a very profound spirit—to incorporeal wisdom, it draws the soul apart in proportion and separates it from the sensible objects of the body by means of its strong agitations. For this reason, Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 CE), a Bishop of Milan and one of the four original Doctors of the Church.</note> says in his book *On the Belief in the Resurrection* <note>original: "livre de la foi de la Resurrection"; referring to the Latin treatise *De fide resurrectionis*.</note>: "Our soul is quite glad to depart from the prison of bodies; it moves with the freedom of the air, without knowing where it comes from or where it goes. We know, nevertheless, that it lives after the death of the body, and that being delivered from the shackles of its own senses, it enjoys a look at freedom; it which did not see at all before while it was enclosed in the body. We can judge this by the example of those who sleep, whose spirits—as if they were resting after the burial of their bodies—rise higher above mortal things, and report back to their bodies those distant and even heavenly things they have seen."

Many doubts, counsels, unknown things, and matters to which one does not give thought—and has never thought—appear clearly to us in our dreams. There, we see representations of places unknown to us, as well as the figures of both the living and the dead. ## Concerning lots, and the signs which have a certain oracular power.

There are also certain lots <note>original: "sorts." What we have said here regarding lots <note>The original OCR reads "forts," but in 17th-century typography, the "long s" (∫) is nearly identical to an "f." The context of biblical "lots" confirms the word is *sorts*.</note> must also be observed for the explanation of signs <note>original: "notes," referring here to symbolic marks or omens.</note>. That is to say, we set out to discern certain marks, though fearing we might err, yet with a strong hope; or perhaps we ask for some sign, as did—according to the Scriptures—Eleazar, the servant of Abraham, and Gideon, a judge in Israel. 

There was anciently in Pharai <note>original: "Pharez," a city in Achaia, Greece, famous for its oracular statue of Hermes described by the traveler Pausanias.</note>, a city in Achaia, an idol of Mercury in the middle of the market. There, anyone who wished to receive an answer regarding what he requested would, after having burned incense and lit the candles that were before the statue, and having placed a local coin as an offering into the belly of the statue, then whisper into the statue’s ear everything he wished to know. Immediately after, blocking his ears with both hands, he would withdraw as quickly as possible from the market. Having left, he would unstop his ears at that very moment, and he would take the first voice he heard as a predestined omen and an oracle rendered to him as an answer to his requests. 

Consequently, although these kinds of lots (as if they depended on chance or fortune) appear to the ignorant to be without cause or reason, God, nevertheless, and the celestial virtues <term>Celestial virtues: in Western esotericism, these are the spiritual hierarchies or angelic powers that transmit divine will through the movements of the stars and earthly events.</term> dispose them for certain reasons, and they do not occur without the intention of their master. 

Was it not thought, when Saul was chosen to be King of Israel, that the lot had fallen upon him by chance and fortuitously? Nevertheless, the Lord had already, before the election, established him as King, and had him given the anointing by the hands of the Prophet Samuel. God, who had made him King, also disposed the lots to make them fall upon him. This is enough on these matters.

# CHAPTER LIII.

->*What preparation is required of one who wishes to receive oracles.*<-

Every person who, intending to reach the sovereign state of the soul <term>Sovereign state of the soul: a term in Neoplatonic and Hermetic philosophy referring to a state of heightened spiritual awareness or "ascent" where the soul is free from bodily distractions and capable of perceiving divine truth.</term>, sets out to seek oracles, must necessarily be assisted and supported by chastity, holiness of life, purity, and cleanliness when presenting themselves; so that their soul is not scabby <note>original: "galeuse," literally "mangy" or "scabby." In this context, it is a metaphor for a soul afflicted by moral corruption or spiritual decay.</note>, nor soiled by any filth, and that no mark or scar of sin is seen imprinted upon their breast. It will also be necessary to entirely detach the mind from common <note>original: "vulgaires," meaning mundane or worldly concerns rather than "crude."</note> things and to purify it, as much as natural necessity permits, from every illness, weakness of spirit, malice, and similar defects, and from every condition contrary to reason which ruins it—just as rust ruins iron. One must put oneself in a good state, preparing everything regarding the tranquility of the mind; for one must be in this state to receive answers from the oracle that possess more truth and effect. To know what is necessary to purify our spirit and restore us to that purity worthy of the presence of God, we must consult religion and wisdom; for one should recognize no religion without wisdom, nor wisdom without religion. For wisdom, says Solomon, is a tree of life for those who have understood it. And

Now, to receive in a single moment gifts of such consequence certainly exceeds the capacity of the human mind; it is therefore necessary for this that the mind be fortified and inspired by the divinity, such as one who is possessed by God, and in whom God operates all things. # CHAPTER LIV.

## *Of cleanliness, and how it must be maintained.*

One must therefore especially maintain this cleanliness <term>cleanliness|The French "netteté" implies both physical hygiene and ritual purity</term> in the way of living, in deeds, in affections, and banish far from oneself all filth and passions of the mind, and everything that displeases the senses and the spirit, and all things within man that are contrary to heaven—not only those in the soul and spirit, but also those in the body, and around the body; for such outward cleanliness, it is believed, contributes not a little to the purity of the spirit. For this reason, the Philosophers of the Pythagorean sect <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who combined mathematics with a mystical, ascetic way of life.</note>, being passionate for the possession of oracles, after having sung the praises of God, would wash themselves in a river or a bath, and dress in robes of white and fine linen; for they considered a woolen garment to be profane, as it is the waste and filth of a beast taken from the flock <note>Pythagoreans avoided animal products like wool, associating them with death and "excrement," preferring plant-based linen for ritual use.</note>. They remained in a pure room, without any dirt or stain. ## CHAPTER LV.

->*Of abstinence, fasting, chastity, solitude, tranquility, and the ascendancy of the spirit.*<-

ABSTINENCE is likewise a preservative and a defense for those who maintain it against vices and evil spirits; it makes of one’s soul a sort of immaculate temple where God dwells, and it unites the spirit to God. For there is nothing better for health and the proper balance of a man’s temperament than not to accumulate excess, and not to exceed that happy medium <term>happy medium|The "Golden Mean" or *aurea mediocritas*, a classical ideal of moderation where one takes only what is necessary for life without falling into gluttony or deprivation.</term> of what is necessary to live. For one must not take nourishment stronger than nature, but rather that which makes nature stronger—as some say of the dog, which regulates its eating so well that nothing superfluous remains in the fourth digestion <note>In traditional Galenic medicine, the "fourth digestion" was the final stage of the metabolic process where nutrients were assimilated into the actual tissues and organs of the body.</note>.

Several others likewise, by eating little, have possessed the pleasure of health and the balance of the body all at once, such as Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty consecutive days;

# CHAPTER LVI.

## *On Penance and Almsgiving.*

The most significant part of purifications <note>term: *purgations* — rituals or internal processes intended to cleanse the soul of material attachments or sins.</note> is voluntary penance for sins. For as Seneca says in *Thyestes* <note>original Latin: "Quem poenitet peccasse paene est innocens" — He who repents of having sinned is almost innocent.</note>, he who repents of his sin is almost innocent; for penance brings us a great absolution by opposing displeasure against pleasure, and because it banishes an animal joy from the soul, and because it gives it a certain particular strength to raise itself from the earth toward heaven. Penance is therefore not only the mortification of vices, but also the spiritual martyrdom of the soul which is pierced on all sides by the sword of the spirit; now this sword of the spirit is the word of God, which causes the Prophet Jeremiah to say, and St. Paul writing to the Ephesians: Cursed be he who keeps back his sword from blood <note>Jeremiah 48:10; here interpreted allegorically as the necessity of spiritual struggle.</note>; and the Psalmist says, his sword is on their lips. This is why it is necessary to declare one's thoughts, and the passions of the mind, and all the evils that come out of our heart and our mouth to the Priest of confession, so that he may judge them according to the word of God, and according to the power he has received from God, and

# CHAPTER LVII.

### *Regarding those things done externally which serve for expiation and justification.*

It has been believed, even by those well-versed in sacred matters, that the soul is also justified by certain institutions and sacraments <term>sacramens</term> administered externally. These include sacrifices, baptisms, exorcisms, blessings, consecrations, and the sprinkling of purified or holy water, as well as certain ointments and perfumes. These are not considered sacred merely because of their ritual use, but because they also naturally possess this virtue. In this manner, sulfur <note>original: "souphre"; used since antiquity in "lustral" or purifying rites to drive away evil spirits through its strong scent.</note> has a place in religious rites, to drive away by its scent—

# CHAPTER LVIII.

## Concerning adorations and vows.

ADORATIONS, vows, sacrifices, and offerings in religious matters are truly steps taken in the search for God; and for those who primarily solicit the will of God, and who wish to establish a commerce <note>original: "commerce"; here meaning a spiritual exchange or communication</note> for the benefit of souls with the gods; for we derive a great power from the prayers and orisons that we utter with true and sacred words, from the sense, and from the spirit, when, by addressing them to some divinity, they move it to address its word and its response to us through a divine ray. By this ray (says St. Denis <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings on "Celestial Hierarchies" were foundational to Western mysticism.</note>), God speaks to men, but in a manner so hidden that they can barely hear it: The King and Prophet David heard and understood it very often; when shall I hear, he said, what the Lord God speaks within me? <note>A reference to Psalm 85:8: "I will hear what God the Lord will speak."</note> Adoration continued for a long time and frequently reiterated thus perfects the understanding and expands the soul to receive divine lights by kindling the love of God, by conferring the gifts of faith, hope, and good morals, and delivers it from everything that is contrary to it and makes war upon it, and also averts many evils which would otherwise happen to it according to the course of natural things. It is for this reason that all antiquity attests that by the virtue of vows, miracles are sometimes performed: healings of diseases, storms turned aside, and other similar wonders. The second thing which is required and necessary for prayer and adoration is a certain resemblance of our life to the divine life proceeding from purity, chastity, and holiness of life, and that the desire for what we ask be equal <note>implying that the seeker's inner intent must match the weight and holiness of the request</note>; for by this means we gain sovereignly the benevolence of God, and we are subjects disposed to receive his liberality. For if we are not worthy through the purity of our spirit to be heard, and even if the things we ask then deserve to be done, it is manifest that the gods do not listen to our prayers. This is what causes the divine Plato to say that through prayers, whatever they may be, we cannot obtain unjust demands from God. Let us then ask nothing of God that we should be ashamed to ask. We see for this reason alone a quantity of people who make prayers and vows in vain, because they are not themselves disposed and prepared according to the maxims of religion, and their wishes and requests are not made for things that are according to the good pleasure of God, and they do not know how to distinguish the order of adoration, and by which mediators one must address God;

AS FOR sacrifice, it is an offering that becomes sacred through the act of presentation, and it sacrifices or sanctifies the person who makes the offering, unless irreverence or some other sin places an obstacle in the way. Through these [natural forces], they make us subject to the influences of fate, and through the former [divine forces], they place us above fate.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For this reason, if some misfortune befalls someone from Saturn or Mars, the Magi <term>Magi: learned practitioners of high magic who studied the relationship between the stars and human affairs</term> command us to have recourse immediately to Jupiter or Venus, rather than to Saturn himself, or to Mars. In this manner, the Psyche of Apuleius <note>Referring to the myth of Cupid and Psyche found in *The Golden Ass* by Lucius Apuleius (2nd century CE).</note>, persecuted by Venus because of her equal beauty, made every effort to merit and obtain her grace—not from Ceres, nor from Juno, but from Venus herself.

# CHAPTER LX.

## **Concerning the requests and the solemnities that the Ancients usually performed while making their sacrifices and presenting their victims to God.**

LET us now see the requests and the prayers that the Ancients made while sacrificing and presenting their victims to God: Here then is what every man who made an <term>oblation<note>A formal offering or gift made to a deity; a ritual act of giving.</note></term> and sacrifice to God would say (or something similar).

> I, your servant, offer and sacrifice these things to you; I recognize you as the author of holiness, and to sanctify myself I invoke this offering, so that through it we may obtain what we ask of you. But furthermore, as this present thing becomes yours through the offering I make of it to you—so that like the rest of the sacrifice, it must live and die only for you—likewise, I myself become a man belonging to you through this offering and <term>communion<note>In this context, the ritual act of sharing in the sacrifice to establish a relationship with the divine.</note></term>. Because I come to offer and sacrifice to you, I confess to you that I am of your family and among your worshipers.

Furthermore, it was said during the <term>immolations<note>The act of killing a victim for sacrifice.</note></term>: just as this animal is in my power to kill it, if I wish, or to save it; so it is in your power to take us away through your anger, or to give— <meta>catchword: -ner (likely "donner," to give)</meta>

...grant through your benevolence what we ask of you. Finally, when the sacrifice was performed for purification, or to turn away some evil, they would say: "just as this animal dies in my hand, so may such and such evil or misfortune die in me and be annihilated; similarly, as the blood of this animal is poured out of its body, so may all vice and all impurity leave me." In the <term>holocaust<note>From the Greek *holokaustos*, meaning "burnt whole." This refers to a sacrifice where the entire offering was consumed by fire, leaving nothing for the priests or the person offering it to eat.</note></term> they would say: "just as this <term>oblation<note>A formal ritual offering or gift presented to a deity.</note></term> is consumed by this present fire, so that nothing remains of it, likewise may all evil be consumed in me, or such and such misfortune that we then wish to repel or turn away."

It was also the custom, when praying and making requests to God, for all those for whom the sacrifice was being performed and who wished to participate in it to touch or hold the altar itself with their hands, because prayer alone cannot sacrifice unless the one who prays also touches the altar with their hands; which is why we read in <term>Virgil<note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE), the Roman poet. Renaissance writers often cited his works like the *Aeneid* as historical evidence of ancient religious rites.</note></term>:

> *The Almighty heard him praying with such words, and holding the altars.* <note>original: "Le Tout-puissant l'entendit priant en telles paroles, & tenant les autels." This is a translation of Virgil's *Aeneid*, IV, 219: *Talibus orantem dictis arasque tenentem audiit Omnipotens*.</note>

And again elsewhere:

> *I touch the altars in the midst of the fires, and I take the deities as witnesses.* <note>original: "Je touche les autels au milieu des feux, & je prens les divinitez à témoins." This is a translation of Virgil's *Aeneid*, XII, 201: *Tango aras, medios ignis et numina testor*.</note>

# CHAPTER LXI.

## *How one must present sacrifices and oblations to the sovereign God, and to the divinities of his celestial court beneath him.*

ALL worship, <term>oblation<note>A formal ritual offering or gift presented to a deity.</note></term>, or sacrifices, as well as requests made through prayers and invocation, are thus distinguished in this way: namely, that they are offered either to God alone, or to lower divinities or powers, such as angels, the stars, and <term>heroes<note>In Renaissance magic, "heroes" refers to "demigods" or exceptional human souls who were elevated to a semi-divine status after death.</note></term>. It is therefore necessary in these matters that you observe such rules: whenever you offer your prayer to God alone to obtain some effect, it should be done with a <term>commemoration<note>The ritual act of recounting or calling to mind a past divine action to empower a current request, effectively saying "as you did then, do so now."</note></term> of some work, miracle, sacrament, or promise taken from some part of the Holy Scriptures. For instance, if the prayer is for the destruction of enemies, one should make commemoration of how God destroyed the giants with the flood of waters; of the [thwarting of the] effort of <term>Babel<note>Referring to the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11), where God confounded human language to prevent the completion of the tower.</note></term> through the confusion of languages; of <term>Sodom and Gomorrah<note>Two biblical cities destroyed by "brimstone and fire" from heaven as divine judgment (Genesis 19).</note></term> under the rain of fire; of the army of Pharaoh in the Red Sea; and similar miraculous expeditions, joining to it all the curses one can gather from the Psalms and the sequence of the Holy Scriptures. In the same way, if we wish to pray to turn away the danger of waters, let us recall how Noah was saved from the flood, and the passage of the Israelites through the...

**And Virgil:**

->*You, my father, take in your hand the sacred things, & the gods of the fatherland.*<-
<note>original: "Tu, genitor, cape sacra manu patriosque Penates." From Virgil's Aeneid, Book II. Aeneas asks his father Anchises to carry the holy icons of Troy because Aeneas, having just come from battle, is ritually "unclean" until he washes in a spring.</note>

From this it follows that the divine **Plato**, in his third book of the **Laws**, commanded that we should honor the statues and sacred images of the gods, not for their own sake, but because they represent the gods to us. In the same way, the Ancients honored the famous idol of **Jupiter**, because it bears the resemblance of man, since the intention is to signify all the things that he produces by the effect of the <term>seed<note>In this context, "seed" refers to the "Logos Spermatikos" or the generative, creative reasons that provide the blueprint for all life in the universe.</note></term>. He is depicted as seated to represent him as a stable and immutable virtue. He is naked and exposed at the top, because he is visible to the superior intelligences and powers; he is covered at the bottom, because he is hidden from the creatures of the lower world. He holds his scepter in his left hand, because the home of life, most full of spirit, is found in those parts of the body <note>A reference to the ancient belief that the heart and the "vital spirits" were centered on the left side of the chest.</note>. He is conceived as the Creator; he is the King and the life-giving spirit of the world. He carries raised in his right hand an **eagle** and a **Victory**; the one because he is the lord of the other gods, just as the eagle is lord of the other birds, and the other because all things are within his power. In this same manner, we also hold in veneration the figure of a **lamb**, because it represents **Christ**, and the figure of a **dove**, because it marks for us the **Holy Spirit**. And the figures of the **ox**, the **lion**, the **eagle**, and the **man** signify the **Evangelists** <note>These four figures, known as the Tetramorph, are derived from the visions in the Book of Ezekiel and the Book of Revelation.</note>, and other similar figures that we find expressed in the revelations of the Prophets in various places of the Holy Scripture. That is why one employs for this purpose everything most beautiful and precious: gold, silver, gemstones, and other things of such importance. This term often referred to turnips or radishes in early modern agriculture; Agrippa is citing ancient agricultural magic where speech was thought to stimulate growth.</note> to grow larger if, when sowing them, one prays for them to do well by ourselves, our family, and our neighbors. Conversely, it has been found that if one sows basil with great insults and maledictions, it bears more beautiful fruit; burned and infused anchovy cures ailments if, while applying it, one does not name it. For this reason Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian historian who frequently wrote on the nature of demons and pagan gods.</note> reports that Serapis in Egypt gave symbols to the public to drive out demons; and that he also taught how demons, taking the form of beasts, set traps for men and surprise them. > If you had faith as large as a grain of mustard seed, nothing would be impossible for you.

# CHAPTER LXV.

## *Conclusion of the Whole Work.*

THIS is what we have gathered in this book to serve as an introduction or entrance to Magic, taken from the tradition of the Ancients, which we have collected and assembled from various authors. The discourse is not long, in truth, but it is long enough for those who will understand it. OCCULT PHILOSOPHY, Book III.

...those considering and looking more subtly than I at these writings, as if in mirrors, and searching with greater devotion into the deepest depths, may find and acquire the perfect doctrines <note>original: "dogmes"</note> and infallible experiments <note>original: "experiences." In this period, "experience" often refers to practical magical operations or scientific trials.</note> of the magical art all together; for we have presented this art in such a manner that it cannot remain hidden from prudent and intelligent men, yet the entrance is not free to the wicked and incredulous who are unworthy of participating in these mysteries and these secrets. Instead, being drawn only to recognize their own stupidity, they shall reject these teachings and leave them behind under the veil of ignorance and the despair of ever seeing or knowing anything within them. It is, therefore, for you and the children of doctrine <note>A traditional term for dedicated students or initiates of a particular philosophy.</note> and wisdom that I have produced this work. Conduct your research in this book by gathering our intention which we have dispersed and proposed in several places; for what we have hidden from you in one place, we have declared to you in another, so that it might be revealed to your wisdom.

For we have written only for you, who possess a pure spirit, instructed and formed to maintain a good order of life; you who, with spirit, chastity, and modesty, and an inviolable faith through the fear and worship of God, do not have hands soiled by sins or crimes, and who are of good character, sober, and modest. For it is you alone who will find the doctrine that we have reserved for ourselves, as well as the secrets veiled by many riddles <note>original: "énigmes"</note> which shall not be uncovered except through a hidden and secret intelligence once you have acquired it. The entire science of this invincible magical discipline <note>A term for the structured study and practice of high magic as a philosophical pursuit.</note> will communicate itself to you in its entirety, and you will see these virtues present themselves to you just as they were acquired in ancient times by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note>, Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, traditionally regarded by Renaissance mages as one of the founders of magic.</note>, Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a first-century Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>, and those other immortal workers of wonders. # OCCULT PHILOSOPHY, Book III.

...the ill-willed, slanderers, subjects of ignorance, and of depraved folly, may they never see your works; for they are against you, and are placed like so many precipices to cast you into error, and to make you miserable. If, therefore, any person—because of his own lack of understanding—does not find what he seeks, let him not impute the fault to my ignorance, and let him not say that I have been mistaken, that I have intentionally written falsehoods, or that I have lied; rather, let him find himself at fault for not understanding our writings. For they are obscure and veiled by many mysteries, where it will happen that many will be deceived, and will lose their way <note>original: "perdront leur latin." A French idiom meaning to be completely bewildered or unable to make sense of something.</note>, and will understand nothing of it. Let no one be angry with us if we have hidden the truth of this science <note>In this context, "science" refers to the "Sacred Science" or the structured system of occult knowledge.</note> under the ambiguity of riddles, and if we have dispersed it in several places throughout this work; for we have not hidden it from the wise, but from perverted and wicked spirits. We have taught it in such a style that it is necessary that the fool understand nothing of it, and that it be understood only by the intelligent man.

*Regarding the true <term>orthodox</term> faith that we must hold toward God, & the most holy Trinity.*

## CHAPTER X.

*Of the divine emanations that the Hebrews call <term>numerations</term>, others call attributes, and the <term>gentiles</term> call gods & deities; together with the ten <term>sephiroth</term>, & the ten most sacred names of God, which preside over them, and their interpretation.*
<note>The term "numerations" is a literal translation of the Hebrew *Sefirot*. The author is harmonizing Jewish Kabbalah with classical paganism ("gentiles") and Christian theology.</note>

## CHAPTER XI.

<note>In Renaissance philosophy, "virtue" (*virtus*) refers to the inherent power, efficacy, or active property of a thing, rather than just moral character.</note>

<note>Original: "medions." This refers to the intermediaries (such as angels or celestial bodies) through which divine power descends into the material realm.</note>

### CHAPTER XV.

*Concerning the opinion of our <term>theologians</term> regarding celestial souls. Page 65*
<note>Theologians here refers to both Christian Church Fathers and Scholastic philosophers. "Celestial souls" refers to the Renaissance belief that the heavenly bodies (stars and planets) possessed living souls or spirits that directed their movements.</note>

### CHAPTER XVI.

*Of <term>intelligences</term> and demons, of their three different kinds, and of their various names; together with infernal and subterranean demons. 67*
<note>In this philosophical system, "intelligences" are purely spiritual, immaterial beings—the highest rank of angels—while "demons" (from the Greek *daimon*) can refer to spirits of various ranks, not exclusively evil ones.</note>

## CHAPTER XXII.

*That every man has three guardian angels, or <term>genies</term>, and from where each of these three genies comes to us. Page 96*
<note>In Renaissance magic, "genies" (from the Latin *genius*) refers to tutelary spirits. This chapter explores the idea that a person is guided by three distinct spirits: one from God, one from the world, and one from their own nature.</note>

## CHAPTER XXIII.

*Of the language of angels, and of their speaking both among themselves and with us. 99*

## CHAPTER XXIV.

*Of the names of spirits and their various <term>impositions</term>; then of the spirits who preside over the stars, the poles of the heaven, and the Elements. 102*
<note>"Imposition" refers to the act of assigning or bestowing a name, often based on the spirit's specific office or power.</note>

## CHAPTER XXV.

*How the <term>Hebrew Doctors</term> derive the sacred names of the Angels from the Holy Scriptures; and concerning the 72 Angels who bear the name of God, together with the <term>Ziruph</term> tables, and of the changes they make to letters and numbers. 107*
<note>"Hebrew Doctors" refers to the Jewish sages and rabbis. "Ziruph" (also spelled *Tziruf*) is a Kabbalistic method of permuting and combining letters of the Hebrew alphabet to reveal hidden meanings or names of power.</note>

## CHAPTER XXVI.

*How one must derive the names of spirits and <term>genies</term> from the arrangement of the celestial bodies. 111*
<note>This chapter connects astrology with spirit-work, suggesting that a spirit's name can be calculated by looking at the positions of the planets and stars at a specific moment, such as a person's birth.</note>

## CHAPTER XXVII.

*Of the art of calculating these types of names according to the tradition of the <term>Cabalists</term>. 114*
<note>The "Cabalists" (Kabbalists) were practitioners of a mystical tradition that sought to understand the relationship between the eternal/mysterious and the finite/mortal universe, often using the numerical values of Hebrew letters.</note>
